triangle-measurement.label: Perpendicular height h
triangle-measurement.description: A triangular shade sail has two anchors along a base b metres long. Its third anchor sits h metres above the line through that base, shifted s metres from its midpoint. Change the height or slide the upper anchor sideways. The dashed height stays perpendicular to the anchor line, even when its foot lies beyond a base endpoint.

triangle-measurement.label: Triangle area and shear primary result
triangle-measurement.description: A triangle has area A equal to half its base b times its perpendicular height h. Slide the third corner sideways while keeping b and h fixed: the triangle changes shape and its sloping sides change length, but its area stays the same. The signed shift s places that corner relative to the base midpoint.

similar-triangles.label: Length scale factor k
similar-triangles.description: A designer begins with a triangular panel whose perpendicular sides are 3 and 4 metres and whose sloping side is 5 metres. The dashed outline keeps that original panel in place. Change one scale factor k to build a similar panel on the same metre scale, then compare its side lengths and material area with the original.

similar-triangles.label: Similar triangles and square-law area primary result
similar-triangles.description: Similar triangles have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding side lengths. Scale a 3–4–5 right triangle uniformly by a positive factor k. Its lengths become 3 k,4 k and 5 k, while area becomes 6 k² square metres. Doubling every length quadruples the enclosed area. The area ratio q equals k²: divide the scaled area by the original six square metres.

perpendicular-bisector.label: Equal compass radius r
perpendicular-bisector.description: A gardener wants a straight border equally distant from two stakes. Set their separation d and draw equal-radius compass circles around them. Their two intersections can be joined by a straightedge. Increase the compass radius and watch those points move apart while the midpoint line stays in the same place.

perpendicular-bisector.label: Stake separation d
perpendicular-bisector.description: A gardener wants a straight border equally distant from two stakes. Set their separation d and draw equal-radius compass circles around them. Their two intersections can be joined by a straightedge. Increase the compass radius and watch those points move apart while the midpoint line stays in the same place.

perpendicular-bisector.label: Perpendicular bisector construction primary result
perpendicular-bisector.description: A perpendicular bisector passes through a segment midpoint at a right angle. Two distinct intersections of equal-radius circles centered at the endpoints lie on this line. If the endpoint distance is d and circle radius is r, each intersection is h=√(r²−d²/4) above or below the segment. The intersection separation is ℓ=2 h.

ellipse-section.label: Semimajor axis a
ellipse-section.description: A garden designer marks two fixed foci, each c metres from the center. A moving boundary marker must keep the total length of its two straight strings to those foci equal to 2 a metres. Change the long half-axis a or focus spacing c, then drag the point parameter t to see the same distance-sum rule at different places on the garden boundary.

ellipse-section.label: Ellipse and focus distances primary result
ellipse-section.description: An ellipse is the locus of planar points whose distances to two fixed foci add to 2 a. Here locus means the set of points satisfying that geometric rule. Put its foci on the horizontal axis at positions −c and c, with vertical coordinate zero and a>c. The semiminor axis is b=√(a²−c²), so enclosed area is A=πab. A moving point with coordinates x=a cos t and y=b sin t keeps the same total focus distance even while its two individual distances change.
